summary:
Liberia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The sodomy offence carries up to one year of imprisonment, applies to women as well as men, and is a domestic-origin provision rather than a colonial import, so no external legal framework presses toward repeal. Same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Enforcement of the sodomy law is uncommon, but its existence deters LGBTQ crime victims from reporting to police, and some LGBTQ people have been arrested on the basis of their sexuality or gender identity after attackers used their LGBTQ status as an excuse.

Legislative pressure on the statute is active. Rep. Johnson N. Williams was seeking lawmakers' support in October 2024 for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill filed that summer, and related proposals would imprison children as young as 10 years old for gay sex. Earlier rounds followed the same pattern: in 2012 new legislation proposed longer jail time for homosexuality and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters, while a bill introduced by then-Senator Jewel Howard Taylor that would have made same-sex marriage a first-degree felony carrying up to ten years passed the Senate but not the House and never became law. President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf had threatened to veto either 2012 anti-LGBTQ bill, and in March 2012 she defended the laws criminalising homosexuality in a joint interview published by The Guardian.

Gender-affirming hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery are not available in Liberia, so a trans visitor cannot obtain transition-related care domestically.

Public concealment is the documented norm: LGBTQ Liberians often have to hide their identities in public, and some private spaces exist where they can be their authentic selves, often sponsored by advocacy organisations such as Stop AIDS in Liberia (SAIL) or the Transgender Network of Liberia (TNOL), or created by private individuals.

One statutory protection exists alongside the criminal law. Section 2.4(b)(iii) of Liberia's Decent Work Act (2015) entitles all who seek to work in Liberia to do so regardless of sex, gender identity or sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
Anti-gay sentiment in Liberia grew after the United States announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas, according to reporting from 9 April 2012; that reporting also described the distribution of fliers targeting gay-rights supporters and new legislation proposing longer jail terms.

A 2013 UN-AIDS survey put HIV/AIDS prevalence among Liberian men who have sex with men at 19.8%. The figure covers MSM rather than trans people specifically and is now more than a decade old.

The UNDP/OHCHR country report 'SOGIR in Africa: Liberia', published in April 2020, is a participatory review of the legal, social and human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia, and provides the most recent structured assessment in this record.

The 2012 statements by President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defending the criminalising laws drew international comment on Liberia's stance; Tony Blair declined to comment in the same interview.
localsOnly:
Stop AIDS in Liberia (SAIL) was the first NGO founded by LGBTQ Liberians for LGBTQ people, set up to educate men who have sex with men about HIV/AIDS, test them and counsel those testing positive, and it expanded its services to all LGBTQ people in 2012. The Transgender Network of Liberia (TNOL) is named alongside SAIL as an organisation sponsoring private spaces for LGBTQ people.

Employment discrimination on grounds of sex, gender identity or sexual orientation is barred by Section 2.4(b)(iii) of the Decent Work Act (2015), a resident-facing entitlement covering anyone who seeks to work in Liberia.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the anti-homosexuality bill filed in the summer of 2024 or the related proposals advancing longer terms and a minimum age of 10 advanced past the support-seeking stage reported in October 2024 is not sourced here; no later legislative outcome is recorded.

No source in this record documents enforcement practice of Section 2.4(b)(iii) of the Decent Work Act (2015), so its availability in practice to a complainant is unresolved.

Whether gender-affirming hormone therapy or surgery has become available since the coverage recording their absence is unresolved; no later clinical source is present.

The record contains no trans-specific homicide or violence figure for Liberia with a population denominator, so no comparative risk magnitude can be stated.
